document.title: Comments of the Solar Energy Industries Association in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s filing to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                   
      ) 
Docket Nos. 
ER26-3515-000 
 
 
 
COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION 
 
Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (Commission),1 the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) submits 
these comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) filing to establish Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS).2  IRAS is a new transmission service that will be 
implemented solely during periods when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand 
in real time operations.3 When triggered, IRAS will enable PJM to prioritize load reduction in 
zones where New Large Loads that have not brought their own new capacity or have their 
capacity needs met through the Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP).4 New Large Loads may 
avoid IRAS by bringing new capacity to the system through the Bring Your Own New Capacity 
(BYONC) construct.5 BYONC would allow New Large Loads that bring new capacity to the 
PJM Region to remove themselves—in whole or in part—from IRAS.6 
SEIA does not take a position on the new transmission service created by PJM’s IRAS 
proposal. These comments address the program that would allow New Large Loads to avoid 
IRAS—the BYONC construct. As the trade association representing both utility-scale and 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2026). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service & a Large Load Registry, 
Docket No. ER26-3515 (Aug. 13, 2026) (IRAS Filing). 
3 IRAS Filing at 1. 
4 IRAS Filing at 1-2. 
5 IRAS Filing at 2. 
6 IRAS Filing at 50.

2 
distribution-scale solar and storage developers in PJM, SEIA submits these comments to provide 
recommendations to the Commission and PJM that would allow Surplus and Distributed Energy 
Resources (DERs) to provide more capacity to the PJM system through a BYONC. 
 
I. 
Comments: To make BYONC more effective, PJM must remove market barriers for 
Surplus and Distributed Energy Resources. 
Under BYONC, the “new” capacity brought to the system “may be supported by 
generation, storage, or demand-side resources that meet certain gating criteria.”7 That gating 
criteria would allow surplus resources and DERs to be part of a BYONC.8 SEIA supports PJM’s 
proposal to allow surplus resources and DERs to qualify for BYONC. In a recent presentation to 
the PJM Load Analysis Subcommittee, Charles River Associates stated that behind the meter and 
co-located resources, like Surplus Resources and DERs, will play a critical near- and medium-
term role in meeting new demand from data centers, especially as structural supply gaps in PJM 
widen.9  
Structural supply gaps cannot be remedied by pricing signals. A strong willingness to pay 
by a developer cannot resolve the significant backlogs facing turbine manufacturers.10 More 
money cannot build transmission faster in the face of significant transformer backlogs.11 PJM 
itself publicly acknowledged in a January 2026 stakeholder meeting that significant new capacity 
 
7 IRAS Filing at 53.  
8 IRAS Filing at 53-54 (“Thus, for generation and storage resources, PJM proposes that the BYONC must be 
supported by:… (3) the incremental capacity created by the utilization of Surplus Interconnection Service. … 
Because capacity may also be supplied by demand-side resources, PJM proposes that BYONC may be supported by 
Planned Demand Resource or Planned Distributed Energy Resources (“DER”) Capacity Aggregation Resources”). 
9 Charles River Associates, Review of Data Center Forecast Methodology, at 20 (Aug. 26, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/subcommittees/las/2026/20260826/20260826-item-04--
charles-river-associates-review-of-data-center-forecast-methodology.pdf (CRA Load Analysis). 
10 Umed Paliwal, Amol Phadke, Existing power plants sharing grid access with new resources can lower costs and 
double PJM’s generation capacity, at 11 (2025), https://surplusinterconnection.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/PJM.pdf 
(Repower PJM). 
11 American Society of Civil Engineers, Infrastructure Report Card, Energy, at 76 (2025), 
https://infrastructurereportcard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Energy.pdf.

3 
additions are unlikely to come online before 2032 due to, among other factors, transmission 
constraints.12 If PJM is going to overcome these supply gaps, then it must use what is available. 
Surplus and distributed resources are the available resources in the near term. Adding 
battery storage to existing wind and solar sites through surplus interconnection could add 13.57 
GW of capacity to PJM.13 This amount of capacity would increase even more if storage were to 
be added to thermal plants as well.14 Capacity from surplus resources can be deployed within 12-
18 months, as opposed to the 5-7 year timeline associated with traditional generation.15 Across 
the PJM region, over 2 GW of distributed energy capacity could be available within just a few 
months.16 Several states across the PJM region have already, or are in the process of, 
implementing programs that would encourage the development of even more distribution-
connected resources.17 But this potential for new capacity can only be unlocked with the right 
market rules in place. PJM must take further action to put those rules in place. 
 
12 See Devin Leith-Yessian, Government-Proposed “Backstop” Auction to Test PJM Stakeholder Process, RTO 
INSIDER (Jan. 26, 2026), https://www.rtoinsider.com/124178-government-proposed-backstop-auction-test-pjm-
stakeholder-process/. (“Even with a backstop auction, [David] Mills [PJM board chair and interim CEO] said there 
are significant barriers to getting new resources built, including transmission upgrades, financing, tariffs, siting, 
permitting and supply chain constraints. Significant new capacity is unlikely to be available until 2032.”). 
13 Repower PJM at 32. 
14 Repower PJM  at 12. 
15 Repower PJM  at 34. 
16 Sunrun, Renew Homes, Tesla, Capacity as a Solution Framework, https://www.vppcapacity.com/, calculated using 
the Capacity Explorer Tool. 
17 About the Legislation: Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA), Ill. Power Agency, 
https://ipa.illinois.gov/crga.html; N.J. Exec. Order No. 2, § 3 (Jan. 20, 2026), 
https://www.nj.gov/infobank/eo/057sherrill/pdf/EO-2.pdf. Maryland Energy Storage Program, Order Initiating 
Workgroup to Develop a Maryland Energy Storage Program, Order No. 90823, Case No. 9715 (Md. P.S.C. Oct. 2, 
2023), http://psc.maryland.gov/wp-content/uploads/Order-initiating-Maryland-Energy-Storage-Program-
Workgroup.pdf. Maryland Energy Storage Program, Order on Investor-Owned Utility Energy Storage Plan 
Proposals in Compliance with the Next Generation Energy Act, Order No. 92281, Case No. 9715 (Md. P.S.C. Apr. 8, 
2026), https://psc.maryland.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/ORDER_1.pdf

4 
A. 
Surplus Resources: Barriers to BYONC Participation and Solutions 
As explained by SEIA, Advanced Energy United, and Google in the Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (RBP) filing, in Docket No. ER26-3380, existing PJM rules limit the ability for 
Surplus Resources to add capacity to the PJM system.18 Currently, PJM only grants capacity 
interconnection rights (CIRs) and capacity accreditation to surplus resources that merge with the 
existing facility as a single hybrid resource,19 a developer seeking capacity value through surplus 
interconnection must elect hybrid treatment—which potentially requires unwinding existing 
financial arrangements. The alternative—interconnecting independently as a co-located 
resource—preserves independent financing but limits the surplus resource to energy-only market 
participation, forfeiting capacity value entirely. Because hybrid treatment requires combined 
market participation as a single resource,20 it does not allow for component-level settlement, and 
capacity performance penalty risk cannot be isolated from the host resource. Lenders to the 
existing facility will rarely consent to the addition of a surplus resource under these conditions, 
because it exposes the existing project to performance liability arising from a resource it does not 
own or control. This effectively renders the surplus interconnection pathway commercially 
unavailable for many projects. 
In the RBP proceeding, SEIA and Advanced Energy United each make recommendations 
on how to resolve these concerns and make the surplus interconnection pathway commercially 
 
18 See Solar Energy Industries Association, Comments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 9-12 (filed Aug. 21, 2026); 
Google LLC, Comments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 10-11 (filed Aug. 21, 2026); Advanced Energy United, 
Comments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 11-15 (filed Aug. 21, 2026). 
19 See PJM Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart E, § 414 (Surplus Interconnection Service); see also Hybrid Resources Market 
Model Selection—Problem Statement, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Aug. 2026) (“Hybrid PS/IC”), available at: 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mic/2026/20260805/20260805-item-04-1---
hybrid-resources-market-model-selection---problem-statement.pdf (recognizing that under current rules, the only 
pathway for surplus resources to obtain capacity value is to become a hybrid resource with the existing project). 
20 See Hybrid PS/IC (discussing issues relating to hybrid resource combined market participation as a single market 
unit in PJM’s energy, capacity, and ancillary services markets).

5 
viable.21 To address these barriers and unlock the significant capacity potential of surplus 
resources, SEIA recommends three reforms. First, PJM should enable surplus resources to obtain 
independently recognized and bankable capacity positions—distinct from the host resource—
without requiring the wholesale restructuring of existing commercial arrangements. This could 
be achieved through several mechanisms, including: (i) split UCAP settlement between 
component accounts; or (ii) CIR transfer mechanisms between co-located resources.22 Whichever 
mechanism is adopted, the objective should be to provide each component of a surplus 
arrangement with independent settlement, revenue allocation, and penalty isolation necessary to 
support separate financing.  
Second, PJM should establish clear protections ensuring that a default or performance 
issue arising from the surplus resource cannot create cross-default risk or otherwise interfere 
with the existing resource’s interconnection agreement or operations. This protection is essential 
to obtaining lender consent: Absent an explicit structural separation of liability, lenders to the 
existing facility will not approve the addition of a surplus resource that could jeopardize the 
project’s existing financing and operational arrangements.  
Third, SEIA encourages PJM to evaluate whether additional resources or process 
modifications can be devoted to surplus interconnection studies to reduce the time from 
application to completion, particularly for projects that could deliver capacity within the RBP’s 
timeframe. The Commission’s acceptance of PJM’s Docket No. ER25-778-000 reforms removed 
 
21 Solar Energy Industries Association, Comments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 9-12 (filed Aug. 21, 2026); 
Advanced Energy United, Comments, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 11-15 (filed Aug. 21, 2026). 
22 Under PJM’s current framework, a surplus interconnection arrangement results in a revised or amended Generation 
Interconnection Agreement for the existing facility, rather than a separate, standalone GIA for the surplus resource. 
See PJM Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart E, § 414(B)(2) (providing that a “revised Interconnection Service Agreement or 
Generation Interconnection Agreement will be prepared and issued to the owner of the existing or planned Generating 
Facility”). This structure means the surplus resource’s market participation, obligations, and potential liabilities are 
housed within the existing project’s agreement, creating the cross-default risk discussed above.

6 
the prior automatic disqualifications that blocked surplus requests. Developers now need PJM to 
complete the studies on time so they can bring resources online in time for the RBP.23 Together, 
these reforms—addressing commercial structure, lender protections, and study timelines for 
surplus interconnection—would enable surplus interconnection to serve as a meaningful near-
term pathway for delivering additional accredited capacity to the PJM system, potentially 
unlocking gigawatts of storage and other resources that are positioned to connect quickly at 
existing points of interconnection. 
SEIA again urges PJM to adopt those recommendations so that New Large Loads can 
actually use surplus resources as new capacity under the BYONC construct. 
B. 
Distributed Energy Resources: Barriers to BYONC Participation and 
Solutions 
In Order No. 2222, the Commission set out to remove the barriers to distributed energy 
resource aggregations participation in wholesale markets.24 Despite the Commission issuing the 
rulemaking in September 2020, implementation of Order No. 2222 is still ongoing. For PJM,  
DER Capacity Aggregation Resources cannot participate in the capacity auction until the 
2028/2029 Base Residual Auction.25 
PJM will allow DER Aggregations to support a BYONC.26 The BYONC construct is a 
program designed to help address the capacity shortfalls that begin in the 2027/2028 Delivery 
 
23 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,083 at PP 30, 33–34 (accepting revisions that expand availability 
of surplus interconnection service and noting that PJM’s proposal “should expand the use of surplus interconnection 
service and allow additional capacity resources to connect to the PJM system”); see also Clean Energy Associations 
Surplus Comments at 3 & n.10. 
24 Participation of Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations in Markets Operated by Regional Transmission 
Organizations and Independent System Operators, Order No. 2222, 172 FERC ¶ 61,247 (2020), order on 
reh'g, Order No. 2222-A, 174 FERC ¶ 61,197 (2021). 
25 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 187 FERC ¶ 61,180, P 1 (2024) (“PJM states that the proposed revisions would 
allow Planned DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to participate in the PJM capacity market beginning with the 
2028/2029 Base Residual Auction (BRA).”). 
26 IRAS Filing at 54.

7 
Year.27 But to participate in a BYONC, the resource must be a Capacity Resource that is 
committed in the capacity auction.28 With capacity market access delayed until the 2028/2029 
delivery year,29 DERs will not be available to participate in a BYONC until a year after the 
BYONC construct begins. And even then, a DER participating in a BYONC must then face the 
additional burden of demonstrating the Accredited UCAP requirement each year in the 10-year 
BYONC period,30 a requirement that is not imposed on other resources participating in a 
BYONC. 
Even after DERs can participate in the capacity market, and in a BYONC, other structural 
limitations impede the ability of New Large Loads to leverage DERs in a BYONC. Several of 
these limitations are actively being litigated in a paper hearing before the Commission.31  
These comments are not intended to relitigate PJM’s Order No. 2222 compliance filing. 
However, given the significant changes in the markets since the Commission initially accepted 
PJM’s initial Order No. 2222 compliance filing, the increasing supply chain and transmission 
constraints facing the PJM region, and the growing interest in DER programs in the region, it 
would be wise for PJM to reevaluate how it can unlock new, and readily available, capacity 
quickly. These comments should serve as guidance to PJM on ways to improve DER access to 
the wholesale markets so that more resources can quickly be made available to New Large 
Loads. 
 
27 IRAS Filing at 6. 
28 IRAS Filing at 55; proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VIII(a). 
29 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 187 FERC ¶ 61,180, P 1 (2024); see also Charles River Associates, Grid Under 
Pressure, at 19 (Feb. 2026), https://media.crai.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/17103809/Grid-under-pressure-
CRA-Energy-Report.pdf. 
30 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI(b)(ii). 
31 See Voltus, Inc., and Mission:data v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,074 (2026).

8 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
The IRAS proposal is another necessary response to PJM’s growing resource adequacy 
issues. But there is much to do to ensure the program is successful. These comments do not 
propose an alternative to what PJM filed. These are recommendations that will allow New Large 
Loads to leverage what is already on the grid, or what can be added quickly, so that PJM can 
unlock the full potential of its proposal. Accordingly, SEIA requests that the Commission and 
PJM consider the market refinements identified in these comments.  
Melissa Alfano  
Senior Director of Energy Markets and Counsel
